headline: Jū, “dwelling”, is from Middle Chinese 住, the goon pronunciation, so likely the initial borrowing.
Udon's origin is uncertain: perhaps from Chinese 餛飩, or a blend of this and 温 (on, “warm”).
Usumeru is the root of 薄い (usui, “thin, dilute”) plus -meru, from Classical Japanese 薄む (usumu).
Igo is 以 (i-, “from... and”) plus 後 (go, “behind; after”).
Tsuyomaru is 強い (tsuyoi, “strong”) plus -maru.
Sutereo is an internationalism; see English stereo.
Makkuro is 真っ (ma'-, “truly”) plus 黒 (kuro, “black”).
Kiji is a Middle Chinese compound, literally “record + affair, event”.
Kuchibiru, “lip”, may come from kuchiberi: 口 (kuchi, “mouth”) plus 縁 (heri, “edge”).
Hibiku is likely derived from a mimetic word, via reduplication.
Kasaneru is from classical 重ぬ (kasanu), from Old Japanese.
Minato is attested in the Nihon Shoki of 720; the traditional etymology is 水 (mi-, “water”) plus な (na) plus 門 (to, “gate”).
Shōgakusei is 小学 (shōgaku, “elementary school”) plus 生 (-sei, “student; pupil”).
Shakai kagaku is 社会 (shakai, “society”) plus 科学 (kagaku, “science”).
Hayai's etymology note is a single pointer: see 早い.
E, a handle, is a change in meaning from 枝 (e, “branch, stem”).
Susumeru, “to advance”, is cognate with 勧める (susumeru) and 薦める (susumeru).
Toku ni is 特 (toku, “special”) plus に (ni).
Senkō is from Middle Chinese 銓衡, and 選考 is a daiyōji replacing 銓衡.
Eru is from Old Japanese, first attested in c. 759 in the Man'yōshū.
Eisei, a satellite, is 衛 (ei, “to guard”) plus 星 (-sei, “celestial body”).
Yawarakai is やわらか (yawaraka, “soft, gentle”) plus い (-i).
Ase is from Old Japanese, from Proto-Japonic *asya.
Bunka is Middle Chinese for “the way of educating by using morality, literature, rituals and music”, repurposed in the Meiji period to translate German Kultur.
Iie shifted from いや (iya), from even earlier 否 (ina), and is first cited to the late 1600s.
Kanshin is 関 (kan, “concern”) plus 心 (shin, “heart”).
Hakase is ultimately from Middle Chinese 博士, an official title in the ritsuryō system, likely borrowed in the Old Japanese period.
Kōsha is 校 (kō, “school”) plus 舎 (-sha, “house”), first attested in 1884.
Ke, “hair”, is cognate with Proto-Ryukyuan *ke (“hair, fur”).
Kangofu is 看護 (“nursing”) plus 婦 (“woman; female”).
Chōsa is chō (調, investigate) plus sa (査, look into).
